title: I tested 9 "the bounce is starting" signals on ~600 crypto coins after sharp drops, including 177 delisted ones. None of them beat the market over the next week.
author: Huge_Position890

comments.author: ciaranwalsh96
comments.body:
This is a strong example of why the resampling unit matters as much as the indicator definition. The day/month clustering point suggests one more robustness check: form the benchmark and uncertainty at the event-date level, not the coin-event level. On a crash day with hundreds of simultaneous signals, those observations are largely one market event, so I would report both the raw event count and the number of independent dates/clusters.



For the “average coin” benchmark, I would freeze the eligible universe at each signal timestamp and consider a value-weighted or liquidity-matched alternative alongside the equal-weighted mean. Otherwise a large set of tiny, distressed coins can dominate the comparison. A leave-one-cluster-out check by month or crash episode would show whether the null result is broad or driven by a few market-wide shocks.



The delisting treatment is conservative in spirit, but last Binance price can still overstate an executable exit when trading or withdrawals deteriorate before delisting. A sensitivity table using the last liquid close, a haircut, and a total-loss bound would make that uncertainty visible. None of these changes need to rescue the signals; they would make the negative result easier to interpret and reproduce.

replies.author: Huge_Position890
replies.body:
Thanks, this was a useful list. I ran all four.

**1. Effective sample.** The 95,719 divergence events fall on 1,679 dates and 57 months. The 1.16M green candles fall on 1,728 dates. I also collapsed everything to one observation per date: signal minus non-signal after controls, each day weighted equally, SE clustered by month. No test reaches SNR 3:

* RSI 0.6
* MACD 1.1
* OBV 1.0
* squeeze −0.8
* sweep + MSB −2.4
* engulfing −1.9

One thing did change. The small positive tilt for sweep + MSB comes from busy days; per day it's slightly negative.

**2. Benchmark.** Four versions of "the average coin" (SNR of the signal effect):

||equal-weight|frozen universe (later delistings at their exit)|dollar-volume weighted|liquidity-quintile matched|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|RSI div|−0.2|0.0|1.1|0.0|
|MACD div|0.5|0.4|0.9|0.6|
|OBV div|0.1|0.3|1.4|0.0|
|squeeze breakout|−1.9|−1.9|−1.4|−1.7|
|sweep + MSB|1.8|1.6|0.1|1.5|
|engulfing|1.2|1.0|−0.5|0.8|

The highest |SNR| anywhere is 1.9.

**3. Leave one month out (57 months).** Dropping a single month never pushes any test past SNR 3. Ranges:

* squeeze: −2.3 to −1.7
* sweep + MSB: 1.6 to 2.1
* engulfing: 0.9 to 1.7
* the three divergences: within ±0.9

Signs only flip for RSI and OBV, which sit at zero anyway.

**4. Delisting exits** (survivorship numbers):

|exit assumption|ended lower|median coin|
|:-|:-|:-|
|last close|88.4%|−84.5%|
|last liquid close (dollar volume ≥ 25% of its own median)|88.2%|−84.5%|
|30% haircut|89.1%|−85.5%|
|total loss|89.7%|−91.3%|

Only the total-loss bound moves the median much.

So the null looks broad. It isn't driven by a few market-wide shocks, by the choice of benchmark, or by the delisting assumption.
